title: BVA Decision 19167246: An effective date earlier than March 2, 2012 for the award of service connection for coronary artery disease (CAD) is denied
text:
Citation Nr: 19167246
Decision Date: 01/28/25	Archive Date: 01/28/25

DOCKET NO. 12-31 116A
DATE: January 28, 2025

ORDER

An effective date earlier than March 2, 2012 for the award of service connection for coronary artery disease (CAD) is denied.

An initial disability rating in excess of 30 percent for service-connected CAD is denied.

A reduction of the 100 percent disability rating for service-connected prostate cancer, effective December 1, 2009, was proper; the appeal is denied.

REMANDED

Service connection for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

?

FINDINGS OF FACT

1. March 2, 2012 is the first date that entitlement to service connection for CAD factually arose under all theories of entitlement raised by the Veteran or reasonably raised by the record.  It was on this date that the evidence, in the form of an echocardiogram, first confirmed the presence of objectively verifiable ischemic heart disease. 

2. For the relevant rating period, the Veteran's service-connected CAD has not resulted in more than one episode of acute congestive heart failure within any 12-month period or chronic congestive heart failure; a workload of 5 metabolic equivalents (METs) or less which resulted in dyspnea, fatigue, angina, dizziness, or syncope; or left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 50 percent or less.

3. The discontinuance of the 100 percent disability rating for the Veteran's service-connected prostate cancer, effective December 1, 2009, was not a formal rating reduction, but a change in rating assignment by operation of law in accordance with 38 C.F.R. § 4.115b, Diagnostic Code (DC) 7528.  The procedural requirements of 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e) were appropriately followed in this case.  The Veteran's prostate cancer was in remission and without continued malignancy at the time of the December 1, 2009 rating reduction.  

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The criteria for an effective date earlier than March 2, 2012, for the award of service connection for CAD, have not been met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 5107, 5110; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.400.

2. The criteria for an initial disability rating in excess of 30 percent for service-connected CAD have not been met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1155, 5107; 38 C.F.R. § 3.102, 4.3, 4.104, DC 7005. 

3. The criteria for the reduction of the 100 percent rating for the Veteran's service-connected prostate cancer, effective December 1, 2009, was proper.  38 U.S.C. § 1155; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.105, 4.115, DC 7528.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

The Veteran served on active duty from February 1969 to September 1970. 

Unfortunately, the Veteran passed away in July 2019 during the pendency of this appeal.  By March 2020 correspondence, the Veteran's daughter was accepted by VA as a valid substitute to see the Veteran's appeal to completion.  As such, the Veteran's daughter is the appellant.  

These matters come before the Board on appeal from October 2007, July 2009, September 2009, and August 2015 rating decisions. 

In February 2016, the Veteran testified before the undersigned Veterans Law Judge (VLJ) at a Board hearing.  The appellant was present at the hearing as an observer.  At this hearing, testimony was taken, in relevant part, on the issues of to service connection for OSA and the propriety of the rating reduction for the Veteran's prostate cancer.  

In September 2016, the Board remanded these claims for further evidentiary development.  In the September 2016 decision, the Board also remanded claims seeking an earlier effective date and a higher rating for the Veteran's CAD for the issuance of a statement of the case (SOC) pursuant to Manlincon v. West, 12 Vet. App. 238 (1999).  

In an August 2019 decision, following the Veteran's death, the Board issued an administrative dismissal of the claims.  The matters have been reactivated before the Board following the appellant's timely and valid substitution.  

Regarding the issues of service connection for OSA and the propriety of the rating reduction for prostate cancer, the appellant has not requested an additional Board hearing following the August 2016 remand of these claims.  See Quinn v. Wilkie, 31 Vet. App. 284 (2019).  

In January 2018, the RO issued an SOC addressing the Veteran's claims seeking an increased rating and an earlier effective date for his service-connected CAD.  The Veteran filed a timely February 2018 VA Form 9, Substantive Appeal, as to these matters and requested a Board hearing.  Such a hearing was not conducted prior to the Veteran's death.  In November 2024, the Board mailed notice to the appellant regarding this outstanding hearing request.  The appellant was notified that if she did not respond within 30 days, the Board would assume she did not wish to attend a Board hearing on these matters.  In a December 2024 letter, the appellant's attorney representative indicated that she wished to withdraw the pending hearing request.  As such, the Board shall proceed with appellate consideration of these matters without the scheduling of a Board hearing.  

In February 2024, the appellant waived her right to have any matter remanded to the RO for initial consideration of any evidence received since the January 2020 SOC.  The SOC addressed the Veteran's prostate cancer rating but largely focused on other matters on appeal.  To the extent that any VA-generated evidence was received between (1) the January 2018 SOC adjudicating entitlement to an earlier effective date and an increased rating for coronary artery disease and the January 2020 SOC or (2) the January 2018 supplemental statement of the case (SSOC) adjudicating the rating reduction issue for prostate cancer and service connection for OSA and the January 2020 SOC, such evidence was either duplicative of evidence already considered by the RO or it was irrelevant to the matters on appeal.  See 38 C.F.R. § 20.1305(c).  Accordingly, the Board may proceed with its appellate consideration. 

The Board notes that a claim of a total disability rating based on individual unemployability (TDIU) was raised during the pendency of this appeal; however, such a claim shall be addressed in a separate Board decision.  

Neither the appellant nor her representative has raised any specific issues with the duty to notify, the duty to assist, or the conduct of the Veteran's February 2016 Board hearing as to the duties discussed in Bryant v. Shinseki, 23 Vet. App. 488, 496-97 (2010).  See Scott v. McDonald, 789 F.3d 1375, 1381 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (holding that "the Board's obligation to read filings in a liberal manner does not require the Board...to search the record and address procedural arguments when the veteran fails to raise them before the Board."); see also Dickens v. McDonald, 814 F.3d 1359, 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2016).  Thus, the Board need not discuss any potential issues in this regard.  

1. An effective date earlier than March 2, 2012 for the award of service connection for CAD.

In an August 2015 rating decision, the Veteran was awarded service connection for CAD, effective March 2, 2012.  On appeal, the appellant seeks an earlier effective date.  Presumably, the appellant seeks an effective date back to November 5, 2009, the date that VA first received the Veteran's informal claim seeking service connection for ischemic heart disease.

Generally, the effective date of an award of disability compensation based on an original claim shall be the date of receipt of the claim or the date entitlement arose, whichever is later.  38 U.S.C. § 5110(a); 38 C.F.R. § 3.400.  However, if the claim is received within one year after separation from service, the effective date of an award of disability compensation shall be the day following separation from active service.  38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1); 38 C.F.R. § 3.400(b)(2)(i).  In this case, the Veteran's claim was not initially filed until many years after his separation from service, so the general rule applies.

While the Veteran filed his claim for a cardiac disability on November 5, 2009, the evidence did not show a clinically significant cardiovascular disease until March 2, 2012.  The regulations dictate that the effective date for service connection is based on the date the claim was filed, or the date entitlement arose, whichever is later.  Here, entitlement did not arise until March 2, 2012, and as such, the RO assigned the proper effective date when it granted entitlement to service connection for coronary artery disease, as discussed below. 

On November 5, 2009, VA first received the Veteran's claim seeking service connection for ischemic heart disease, claimed as due to service in the Republic of Vietnam.  In September 2009, the Veteran underwent a cardiac stress test.  The results of the testing showed no scintigraphic evidence of ischemia.  The stress test results were interpreted by a private cardiologist in September 2009, who stated that there was no evidence of active ischemia.  The cardiologist did not list any heart conditions in the assessment section of his report.  An echocardiogram was conducted in October 2009, and it demonstrated normal left ventricular function, a slightly enlarged left ventricle, and no significant valve abnormalities.  See March 2010 private records.  The Veteran was not assessed with a clinically significant cardiovascular disorder.  

In December 2010, the Veteran submitted private primary care records which did not identify the presence of ischemic heart disease or CAD during the rating period.  In the December 2010 rating decision, the RO denied entitlement to service connection for ischemic heart disease.  The RO explained that while the evidence showed reports of chest pain, the medical records did not show clinically identifiable ischemic heart disease.

In November 2009, March 2010, June 2010, March 2011, and June 2011, the Veteran visited his VA primary care provider, who documented a comprehensive list of the Veteran's active medical problems.  These records did not include any notations diagnosing the Veteran with a clinically significant cardiac condition, such as ischemic heart disease or CAD.  In fact, these records primarily documented the Veteran's denial of chest pain and/or palpitations.  

To the extent that the Board has relied on the absence of evidence of a clinically significant cardiac disability in the treatment records identified above, the Board is cognizant that an absence of documented complaints in a medical record cannot always constitute substantive negative evidence.  See Buczynski v. Shinseki, 24 Vet. App. 221, 224 (2011).  In order to find that silence in the record is probative, the Board "must first establish a proper foundation for drawing inferences against a claimant from an absence of documentation."  Fountain v. McDonald, 27 Vet. App. 258, 272 (2015) (citing Horn v. Shinseki, 25 Vet. App. 231, 239, n.7 (2012) for the proposition that "the absence of evidence cannot be substantive negative evidence without 'a proper foundation to demonstrate that such silence has a tendency to prove or disprove a relevant fact.'").  Such a foundation may be laid by a finding that the fact at issue would ordinarily have been recorded, in which case the Board may legitimately infer from the absence of such a record that it did not occur.  See id.; Buczynski, 24 Vet. App. at 224 (noting that under Federal Rule of Evidence 803(7), "the absence of an entry in a record may be evidence against the existence of a fact if such a fact would ordinarily be recorded").  

In the present case, the lack of reference to ischemic heart disease or CAD in the private cardiology records and/or the VA primary care records prior to March 2, 2012 is probative.  A cardiologist is a physician who specializes in identifying, diagnosing, and treating cardiovascular disorders.  Following the procurement of necessary testing, the cardiologist did not identify atherosclerotic heart disease until the April 2012 treatment visit.  Given his level of expertise, and the role that cardiologists play in diagnosing heart conditions, it is reasonable to conclude that if the Veteran had ischemic heart disease or coronary artery disease, the private cardiologist would have documented such findings in the Veteran's treatment records earlier than March 2, 2012 if such a diagnosis was medically indicated by diagnostic testing.  It was not until the cardiologist interpreted the March 2012 echocardiogram and the April 2012 stress test that he determined that the Veteran met the diagnostic criteria for atherosclerotic heart disease.  

Likewise, the treatment records from the Veteran's primary care provider contained detailed assessments of the Veteran's present symptoms, chief complaints, and his active medical problems.  As these reports were thorough in nature and based on an assessment of the Veteran's medical history, it is reasonable to conclude that the primary care provider would have listed ischemic heart disease or CAD as an active medical problem, if such a disease was medically indicated.  The absence of such documentation until after March 2, 2012 is probative in this appeal.

The medical evidence in existence prior to March 2, 2012 failed to demonstrate the presence of ischemic heart disease or CAD, and without a current disability for VA compensation purposes, entitlement to service connection could not have arisen any earlier than March 2, 2012 under any applicable theory of entitlement.

A current cardiovascular disability was not established until a March 2, 2012 echocardiogram was performed.  In April 2012 treatment records, the Veteran's private cardiologist interpreted the Veteran's recent echocardiogram, as well as recent Persantine thallium stress test results, and for the first time, diagnosed the Veteran with arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease.  This was the first time in the record that a clinical diagnosis of a cardiac disability was identified on a facts found basis.  

The Veteran first filed a claim seeking entitlement to service connection for ischemic heart disease on November 5, 2009.  The Veteran did not submit any formal or informal communications to VA prior to November 5, 2009 indicating an intent to apply for service connection for a cardiac disability.  See Criswell v. Nicholson, 20 Vet. App. 501, 503 (2006).  While the date of claim is November 5, 2009, the Veteran did not have ischemic heart disease or coronary artery disease for VA compensation purposes until March 2, 2012, which is, therefore, the date entitlement arose and the earliest possible effective date for the grant of service connection for such a disability.  There is no competent medical evidence proving that the Veteran had ischemic heart disease or CAD for VA compensation purposes prior to March 2, 2012.   

Although the appellant's attorney included boilerplate references to the RO's "fail[ure] to assist in the development of the claim, fail[ure] to appropriately analyze the entire record of evidence, and fail[ure] to apply the 'benefit of the doubt rule,'" in argument attached to the February 2018 VA Form 9, he did not note any specific deficiencies in this case.  He also did not submit any substantive argument explaining why the appellant believes an effective date earlier than March 2, 2012 is warranted for the Veteran's award of service connection for CAD, nor did he cite any specific evidence in support of his claim.

Consistent with the above analysis, March 2, 2012 is the date the evidence first showed a clinically identifiable cardiac disability for VA compensation purposes, and thus, this is the date that entitlement to service connection first arose.  Prior to this date, the current disability element of a viable service connection claim was missing.  The RO assigned the proper effective date of March 2, 2012 for the award of service connection for coronary artery disease.  The evidence is not in approximate balance and persuasively weighs against the appellant's claim.  As such, the benefit-of-the-doubt doctrine is not for application.  See 38 U.S.C. §5107(b); 38 C.F.R. § 3.102; see also Lynch v. McDonough, 21 F.4th 776, 780-82 (2021).  Therefore, an effective date earlier than March 2, 2012 for the award of service connection for CAD, is not warranted. 

2. An initial disability rating in excess of 30 percent for service-connected CAD. 

During the relevant rating period, the Veteran was in receipt of a 30 percent rating for his CAD under DC 7005, 38 C.F.R. § 4.104.  On appeal, the appellant seeks a higher initial disability rating. 

During the pendency of the appeal, the rating criteria for evaluating cardiovascular disorders under 38 C.F.R. § 4.104 were amended, effective November 14, 2021.  86 Fed. Reg. 54089 (Sept. 30, 2021).  As the Veteran died in 2019, prior to the amendments in question, the revised regulations are not for application.  

Under the pre-amended rating criteria for DC 7005, a higher 60 percent rating is warranted where there is documented coronary artery disease resulting in more than one episode of acute congestive heart failure in the past year, or; a workload of greater than 3 METs but not greater than 5 METs resulting in dyspnea, fatigue, angina, dizziness, or syncope, or; left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 30 to 50 percent.  A maximum 100 percent is warranted for documented coronary artery disease resulting in chronic congestive heart failure, or; workload of 3 METs or less results in dyspnea, fatigue, angina, dizziness, or syncope, or; left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of less than 30 percent.  One MET (metabolic equivalent) is the energy cost of standing quietly at rest and represents an oxygen uptake of 3.5 milliliters per kilogram of body weight per minute.

The Veteran's CAD was rated under DC 7005, 38 C.F.R. § 4.104, and neither the Appellant nor her attorney has challenged the use of this DC to rate the Veteran's disability or cited to any other diagnostic code that would be more appropriate to rate the Veteran's disability.  As such, the Board shall proceed with the adjudication of this appeal utilizing the rating criteria set forth in the pre-amended version of DC 7005.

In consideration of the evidence, the Board finds that the Veteran's cardiac condition never manifested itself as acute or chronic congestive heart failure.  From March 2, 2012 through the Veteran's date of death, the evidence does not show that his CAD resulted in a workload of 5 METs or less resulting in dyspnea, fatigue, angina, dizziness, or syncope; or left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 50 percent or less.  The March 2, 2012 echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55 to 60 percent.  The stress test conducted in April 2012 showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 51 percent.  The Veteran had a VA cardiology consultation in May 2016 to get clearance to undergo a total knee replacement.  The clinician noted that echocardiograms from 2015 and 2016 showed left ventricular hypertrophy.  The Veteran denied chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, syncope, or palpitations.  The clinician identified no active concerns. 

The evidence fails to demonstrate that the Veteran experienced the symptoms or medical findings needed to achieve a rating higher than 30 percent for his service-connected CAD during the relevant rating period.  

Although the appellant's attorney included boilerplate references to the RO's "fail[ure] to assist in the development of the claim, fail[ure] to appropriately analyze the entire record of evidence, and fail[ure] to apply the 'benefit of the doubt rule,'" in argument attached to the February 2018 VA Form 9, he did not note any specific deficiencies in this case.  He did not cite to any evidence of record showing that the Veteran satisfied the regulatory criteria for a rating higher than 30 percent under the pre-amended version of DC 7005.

In sum, the Board finds that the evidence weighs against a rating higher than 30 percent for the Veteran's service-connected CAD for the period between March 2, 2012 and his death in July 2019.  The evidence is not in approximate balance and persuasively weighs against the appellant's claim.  As such, the benefit-of-the-doubt doctrine is not for application.  See 38 U.S.C. §5107(b); 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 4.3; see also Lynch, 21 F.4th at 780-82.  Therefore, an initial disability rating in excess of 30 percent for service-connected CAD is not warranted.  

3. The propriety of the reduction of the 100 percent disability rating for service-connected prostate cancer, effective December 1, 2009.

The appellant contends that the reduction of the Veteran's evaluation for prostate cancer from 100 percent disabling to 20 percent, effective December 1, 2009, was improper. 

The Veteran's prostate cancer was rated DC 7528, 38 C.F.R. § 4.115b.  The Board notes that the criteria for evaluating genitourinary system disabilities were amended, effective November 14, 2021, however these amendments did not impact DC 7528.  See 86 Fed. Reg. 54081 (Sept. 30, 2021).  

Under DC 7528, malignant neoplasms of the genitourinary system are evaluated as 100 percent disabling.  38 C.F.R. § 4.115b, DC 7528.  A note to this provision indicates that following the cessation of surgical, x-ray, antineoplastic chemotherapy or other therapeutic procedure, the rating of 100 percent will continue with a mandatory VA examination at the expiration of 6 months.  Any change in evaluation based upon that or any subsequent examination shall be subject to the provisions of § 3.105(e) of this chapter.  If there has been no local reoccurrence or metastasis, rate on residuals as voiding dysfunction or renal dysfunction, whichever is predominant.  Id. 

The phrase "the cessation of surgical, X-ray, antineoplastic chemotherapy or other therapeutic procedure," in 38 C.F.R. § 4.115b, DC 7528, refers to the cessation of treatment for the applicable malignant neoplasm of the genitourinary system.  Thus, the 100 percent rating will end as of the date the veteran received final treatment for cancer, the cessation of treatment for the cancer itself, as opposed to treatment for residuals secondary to the cancer or further treatment required as a result of the treatment for the disease.  See Tatum v. Shinseki, 26 Vet. App. 443, 447-48 (2014) (also referred to as "Tatum II").

The rating reduction provisions of 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.343 and 3.344 are not applicable in the present case.  See Love v. McDonough, 106 F.4th 1361, 1368-70 (Fed. Cir. 2024); Foster v. McDonough, 34 Vet. App. 338, 345-46 (2021);.  Here, the discontinuance of the 100 percent disability rating for service-connected prostate cancer was accomplished pursuant to the provisions of 38 C.F.R. § 4.115b, DC 7528.  In that regard, DC 7528 contains a temporal element for continuance of a 100 percent rating for prostate cancer or its residuals.  Therefore, the action taken by the RO was not a "rating reduction," as that term is commonly understood.  See Foster, 34 Vet. App. at 345-46.  Rather, the rating reduction in this case was procedural in nature and by operation of law.  The only requirement is that once the appropriate examination shows cancer remission, any change in the disability rating is subject to the procedural requirements of 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e).  A reduction implemented pursuant to 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e) requires a 60-day notice before VA reduces an evaluation and an additional 60-day notice before the reduced evaluation takes effect.

By way of background, a July 2006 rating decision granted entitlement to service connection for prostate cancer and assigned a 100 percent rating based on active malignancy, effective April 4, 2006.  The Veteran was notified that the 100 percent rating would continue with a mandatory VA examination at the expiration of 6 months.  Any changes to evaluation based on reexamination were subject to 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e), and if there was no local recurrence or metastasis, his residuals would be rated based on voiding dysfunction or renal dysfunction, whichever was predominant.  

The Veteran attended a VA prostate examination in June 2007, and in October 2007, the RO continued a 100 percent rating because the Veteran remained under treatment for active malignancy. 

The Veteran attended another VA prostate examination in December 2008.  It was noted that the Veteran's treatment was complete, and his last treatment date was May 22, 2008.  The Veteran's malignancy was noted as being in full remission for 7 months.  In January 2009, the RO issued a rating decision proposing to reduce the Veteran's rating for prostate cancer from 100 percent to 10 percent.

In a September 2009 rating decision, the RO decreased the Veteran's 100 percent rating for his service-connected prostate cancer to 10 percent, effective December 1, 2009.  In a January 2018 rating decision, the RO increased the Veteran's disability rating for his prostate cancer to 20 percent, from December 1, 2009 through August 21, 2014.  The practical effect of the January 2018 rating decision is that the Veteran's disability rating for prostate cancer was reduced from 100 percent to 20 percent, effective December 1, 2009. 

Regarding the issue of the effective date of the reduction, it appears that the RO complied with the procedural requirements of 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e).  The reduction was made effective no sooner than permitted by current law and regulations ("the last day of the month in which a 60-day period from the date of notice to the beneficiary of the final action expires").  38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e).  Specifically, the Veteran was notified of the proposed reduction in a January 13, 2009 rating decision and a January 22, 2009 notice letter.  In February 2009, the Veteran submitted a lay statement alleging an hourly daytime voiding interval when drinking liquids and awakening every two hours to void.  This evidence did not show continued malignancy of the prostate.  The Veteran did not request a personal hearing within 30 days of the January 22, 2009 notice letter.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(i).  More than 60 days passed before the RO issued a rating decision implementing a rating reduction. 

In the September 16, 2009 rating decision, mailed to the Veteran on September 24, 2009, the Veteran was notified that the 100 percent evaluation was being decreased to 10 percent, effective December 1, 2009.  As December 1, 2009 fell after the 60-day period from the date of the September 24, 2009 notice to the beneficiary of the final action, the Board finds the December 1, 2009 effective date for the rating reduction to be proper.  The RO properly complied with the procedural requirements of 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e).

The next question is whether the reduced rating was supported by the evidence of record.  As noted above, the Veteran attended a VA examination in December 2008.  A rectal examination was performed, and the prostate was within normal limits, and there were no anal hemorrhoids, fissures, or masses.  An examination of the genitals was also normal.  The examiner noted that treatment for the Veteran's prostate cancer ceased in May 2008 and the Veteran had been in remission for 7 months.  Thus, the Veteran no longer had active malignancy in the prostate.

In the brief attached to the September 2012 Notice of Disagreement and at the February 2016 Board hearing, the Appellant's counsel argued that the reduction was improper because the Veteran's prostate cancer precluded the Veteran from engaging in gainful activity.  The attorney argued that VA failed to consider whether the Veteran could return to work following his prostate cancer treatment.  The attorney stated that VA's Adjudication Procedures Manual (also known as the M21-1) required VA to adjudicate whether a veteran could return to work prior to reducing a rating.  He did not cite a specific provision from the M21-1 in support of his claim, and the Board's independent review of the manual has failed to identify any provisions correlating to the attorney's argument.  The rating reduction requirements under 38 C.F.R. § 4.115b, DC 7528 do not involve an inquiry into whether the Veteran could return to substantially gainful employment.  This argument is directed more towards the Veteran's claim seeking a TDIU, which is addressed in a separate decision.  Consequently, the attorney's argument holds no weight for this issue. 

Overall, the evidence shows that the Veteran's prostate cancer had been in remission for several months by the time of the December 2008 VA examination, and the Veteran completed his prostate cancer treatment in May 2008.  The procedural requirements of 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(e) were followed.  As the evidence reflected no local reoccurrence or metastasis of prostate cancer from December 1, 2009, the 100 percent evaluation for prostate cancer was properly reduced.  See 38 C.F.R. § 4.115b, DC 7528; Foster, 34 Vet. App. At 344-49.  The issue of an increased rating for the Veteran's prostate cancer following the reduction of his 100 percent rating shall be addressed in a separate Board decision. 

REASONS FOR REMAND

1. Service connection for OSA.

In an October 2007 rating decision, the Veteran was denied service connection for OSA, in part, due to the lack of a current disability.  VA treatment records from February 2008 showed that the Veteran was prescribed equipment for OSA.  This evidence is new, as it was not in existence at the time of the October 2007 rating decision, and it is material, as it pertains to an unestablished fact necessary to substantiate the claim, namely the presence of a current disability for VA compensation purposes.  The claim has remained pending since the June 2007 informal claim, which was initially adjudicated in the October 2007 rating decision.  

In September 2016, the Board remanded the matter for a VA examination and medical opinion addressing whether the Veteran's OSA was caused or aggravated by his service-connected prostate cancer.  In January 2018, the RO determined that an in-person examination was not required because a diagnosis of OSA was well-established by the medical evidence.  The RO referred the matter to a VA examiner for a medical nexus opinion.  In January 2018, a VA examiner issued a comprehensive medical opinion explaining why the Veteran's OSA was not caused by his prostate cancer.  The Board finds this VA medical opinion to be thoughtfully explained, supported by an explanatory rationale, and adequate to resolve the secondary causation theory of entitlement.  

The January 2018 VA examiner did not address whether the Veteran's OSA was aggravated by his service-connected prostate cancer, as requested by the September 2016 Board remand.  See Stegall v. West, 11 Vet. App. 268, 271 (1998) (holding that claimants are entitled to compliance with Board remand instructions).  A medical opinion that addresses only causation and not aggravation is inadequate to adjudicate a claim for service connection on a secondary theory of entitlement based on aggravation.  See El-Amin v. Shinseki, 26 Vet. App. 136, 140 (2013); see also Atencio v. O'Rourke, 30 Vet. App. 74, 91 (2018) (causation and aggravation are independent concepts and should have separate findings and rationales).  The claim must be remanded for an addendum medical opinion addressing the aggravation prong of a secondary service connection claim.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.310(b).  

At the time of the September 2016 Board remand, there was no evidence or allegation that the Veteran's OSA was incurred in or otherwise etiologically related to his active duty service.  However, on August 10, 2022, during the pendency of this appeal, the United States President signed into law the Sergeant First Class Heath Robinson Honoring our Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxics Act of 2022, Pub. L. No. 117-168 (codified as amended in scattered sections of 38 U.S.C.),136 Stat. 1759 (2022) (PACT Act).  The PACT Act created 38 U.S.C. §1168(a) setting forth criteria for when VA has a duty to assist in obtaining a medical nexus examination for veterans with a qualifying toxic exposure risk activity (TERA).  Under this statute:

[I]f a veteran submits to the Secretary a claim for compensation for a service-connected disability under section 1110 of this title with evidence of a disability and evidence of participation in a toxic exposure risk activity during active military, naval, air, or space service, and such evidence is not sufficient to establish a service connection for the disability, the Secretary shall-

(A) provide the veteran with a medical examination under section 5103A(d) of this title; and

(B) obtain a medical opinion (to be requested by the Secretary in connection with the medical examination under subparagraph (A)) as to whether it is at least as likely as not that there is a nexus between the disability and the toxic exposure risk activity.

38 U.S.C. § 1168(a)(1).

The health care provider [providing the medical nexus opinion] shall consider:

(A) the total potential exposure through all applicable military deployments of the veteran; and

(B) the synergistic, combined effect of all toxic exposure risk activities of the veteran.

38 U.S.C. § 1168(a)(2).

The Veteran's service personnel records establish that he served in the Republic of Vietnam during the time period when herbicide agents were used.  See also July 2006 rating decision (conceding in-service herbicide agent exposure).  Thus, pursuant to 38 C.F.R. § 3.307(a)(6)(iii), in-service exposure to herbicide agents is legally presumed.  

As the Veteran's in-service herbicide agent exposure qualifies as a valid TERA, the RO has a statutory obligation to obtain a VA examination and medical nexus opinion addressing the etiology of the Veteran's OSA and whether it is related to the Veteran's TERA.  OSA is not one of the disabilities determined by the Secretary to have no positive association with herbicide agents, such that a TERA examination is not warranted.  See VBA Letter 20-24-06, Updated Guidance on Processing Claims Involving the PACT Act, at *12-13, 89 Fed. Reg. 51,224 (June 17, 2024).  As the Veteran is deceased and therefore cannot attend an in-person examination, the Board finds that VA's duty to assist obligations are limited to obtaining a relevant VA medical opinion.  Accordingly, the claim must be remanded for the procurement of a TERA medical nexus opinion in compliance with the PACT Act.

The matter is REMANDED for the following action:

Obtain an addendum VA medical opinion from an appropriate VA examiner regarding the etiology of the Veteran's OSA.  Following a complete review of the electronic claims file, including a copy of this REMAND, the VA examiner is requested to address the following inquiries:

(a.) Is it at least as likely as not (likelihood is at least approximately balanced or nearly equal, if not higher) that there is a nexus between the Veteran's OSA and his TERA of being exposed to herbicide agents during his active duty service?

(b.) Is it at least as likely as not (likelihood is at least approximately balanced or nearly equal, if not higher) that the Veteran's OSA was aggravated (i.e., underwent any incremental increased in disability, regardless of its permanence) by his service-connected prostate cancer?

Ensure that all medical opinions issued by the VA examiner are accompanied by complete rationales based on the examiner's clinical experience and medical expertise; established medical principles; and/or citations to the electronic claims file, as appropriate.

 

 

RYAN T. KESSEL

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Galante, M.

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided.  This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability.  38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.
